title: Observation of measurement-induced localization phenomena in a solid-state spin system
authors: Haolin Zhang, Shaoyi Xu, Zihang Zheng, Mengqi Wang, Mingzhe Liu, Zhiyuan Zhao, Ya Wang, Tianyu Xie, Fazhan Shi
abstract: Quantum measurement can profoundly impact the dynamics of many-body systems, for instance, inducing phase transitions from volume-law chaotic phases to area-law localized phases. While chaotic phases emerge naturally in generic many-body systems, the experimental realization of a fully localized phase driven by measurement remains challenging, primarily owing to the stringent requirement of near-perfect isolation of the system from environmental dissipation. Here we experimentally observe measurement-induced localization phenomena in an interacting $^{13}\mathrm{C}$ nuclear spin system in diamond. In contrast to previous circuit-model-based experiments, our well-isolated system evolves under a physical many-body Hamiltonian with measurements intervening at intervals. By implementing either projective measurements on a single spin or global weak measurements on the entire system, we observe substantially prolonged spin autocorrelation times as the measurement frequency increases. Our results, combined with numerical simulations, provide evidence that quantum measurement can drive a many-body system into a localized regime, and lay the groundwork for future experimental investigations into measurement-induced many-body dynamics and related entanglement phenomena.
summary: This paper reports the experimental observation of measurement-induced localization (MIL) in a solid-state $^{13}	ext{C}$ nuclear spin system embedded in diamond. By applying controlled projective and weak measurements, the researchers demonstrated that the system's dynamics transition from a chaotic, volume-law regime to a localized, area-law regime. This work validates the theoretical understanding of measurement's role in controlling many-body quantum phases.
main_problem: The primary goal is to experimentally observe and demonstrate measurement-induced localization (MIL) in a solid-state spin system, contrasting with the difficulty of realizing such fully localized phases.
main_result: The authors successfully observed MIL by showing that increasing the measurement frequency (via projective or weak measurements) substantially prolongs the spin autocorrelation time, driving the system into a localized regime.
method: The experiment uses an interacting solid-state $^{13}	ext{C}$ nuclear spin system in diamond, read out via an adjacent NV center, and measures the spin autocorrelation function under varying measurement strengths.
model_or_system: The system is an interacting $^{13}	ext{C}$ nuclear spin network governed by a dipolar Hamiltonian, evolving towards a volume-law chaotic phase. Measurements are implemented either projectively on a single spin or globally weakly on the entire system.
key_observables: Spin autocorrelation function ($\langle\sigma_z(0)\sigma_z(t)angle$), which shows prolonged decay times indicating localization.
important_parameters: Measurement frequency (or strength $\gamma$), which controls the transition between chaotic and localized dynamics.
main_assumptions: The system is well-isolated, allowing the physical many-body Hamiltonian to govern dynamics between measurement interventions.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the transition from volume-law chaotic evolution to localized behavior under measurement, and show the baseline decay curves and the effect of measurement frequency on autocorrelation time.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the theoretical context of MIL, details the physical setup using the diamond spin system, presents the measurement protocols (projective vs. weak), and finally reports the observation of prolonged autocorrelation times as evidence for measurement-induced localization.
why_interesting: This work provides a direct experimental realization of a theoretical concept (MIL) in a solid-state platform, offering crucial insights into how measurement back-action can fundamentally alter many-body quantum dynamics, which is highly relevant to open quantum systems.
